subtopics.title: What Turns Rain into a Flood — Physical Causes

questions.question: Fifty millimetres of rain in one hour is more dangerous than the same fifty over a week because:
options: Weekly rain contains less water
Intense rain overwhelms the ground's ability to absorb it, so most becomes immediate runoff
Rain gauges cannot measure hourly rain
Slow rain evaporates before landing

questions.question: A cut-off low causes major floods because it:
options: Brings freezing temperatures
Blows rivers backwards
Only forms over the ocean
Breaks away from the upper westerlies and stalls, wringing rain over the same region for days

questions.question: Antecedent moisture matters because a saturated catchment:
options: Turns almost all further rain directly into runoff
Absorbs more rain than a dry one
Cannot receive any more rainfall
Cools the air above it

questions.question: A compact, round catchment tends to produce higher flood peaks than a long narrow one because:
options: It receives more rainfall in total
Its rivers flow uphill
All its water arrives at one point at nearly the same time, stacking the flow
It has no vegetation

questions.question: Urbanisation increases flooding chiefly because:
options: Cities attract more rainfall
City rivers are narrower than rural ones
Urban trees drink too much water
Tar, rooftops and paving seal the ground, and stormwater drains deliver runoff to rivers fast

questions.question: Destroying a wetland worsens floods because a wetland:
options: Is a natural sponge that stores floodwater and releases it slowly
Blocks rivers from flowing
Increases evaporation
Attracts thunderstorms

questions.question: Deforestation and overgrazing add a second injury beyond faster runoff:
options: They lower the water table permanently
Eroded silt settles in channels and dams, raising riverbeds and shrinking flood capacity
They increase rainfall intensity
They attract cut-off lows

questions.question: Flood risk in South Africa is distributed by inequality means:
options: Wealthy suburbs flood most often
Floods only strike rural areas
Those with the least choice — informal settlements — occupy the most dangerous flood-prone land
Insurance covers all flood damage equally

subtopics.title: The Flood Hydrograph, Described in Words

questions.question: On a flood hydrograph, the axes show:
options: Rainfall against temperature
Time on the horizontal axis and discharge in cumecs on the vertical axis
Distance downstream against river depth
Wind speed against rainfall

questions.question: Base flow is:
options: The river's everyday flow, fed by groundwater seeping into the channel
The lowest point of the flood peak
Water flowing under the riverbed
The storm's first surface runoff

questions.question: Lag time is the interval between:
options: Two successive storms
The start and end of rainfall
Base flow and the rising limb
The heaviest rainfall and peak discharge

questions.question: The falling limb descends more gently than the rising limb climbed because:
options: The rain usually starts again
Evaporation slows after a storm
The last water arrives by slower routes — through the soil and from the furthest parts of the catchment
Measuring stations record falling water badly

subtopics.title: Reading Hydrographs — Urban Against Rural, Flash Against Regional

questions.question: Compared with a rural vegetated catchment in the same storm, an urbanised catchment's hydrograph shows:
options: A longer lag and lower peak
A shorter lag, a higher narrower peak and steeper limbs
No change in shape
A higher base flow between storms

questions.question: The rural sponge catchment keeps a persistent base flow between storms because:
options: Its stormwater drains store water
Its rivers are dammed
Rain evaporates more slowly there
Infiltrated water recharges groundwater, which keeps feeding the channel

questions.question: The Laingsburg flood of January 1981 was a flash flood because:
options: A cut-off low dumped over 400 mm in about two days onto bare rocky catchments, giving almost no lag time
It lasted several weeks across many provinces
It was caused by a dam failure
It happened at the coast during a cyclone

questions.question: A regional flood, like KwaZulu-Natal in April 2022, differs from a flash flood by:
options: Being caused only by burst pipes
Never causing deaths
Building over one to several days across a wide area, slower to arrive but vast in extent and duration
Peaking within minutes in a single valley

subtopics.title: The Sponge and the Corrugated Roof

questions.question: In the yard experiment, the corrugated iron sheet represents:
options: Surfaces that reject infiltration — rock, baked or saturated ground, and the paved city
A wetland storing floodwater
Deep sandy soils
A vegetated catchment

questions.question: A full sponge IS a sheet of iron means:
options: Sponges harden when dry
Wetlands turn to rock over time
Iron absorbs water when rusted
A saturated catchment sheds the next storm as if it were sealed

questions.question: Intensity beats total means:
options: The biggest storms always have the most water
A hard hour of rain that outpaces the ground's drinking speed floods where the same water as all-day drizzle would soak away
Total rainfall is never measured
Drizzle causes the worst floods

questions.question: Real rivers still flow in the dry season because:
options: Dams release water daily
Sea water pushes upstream
Base flow — groundwater seeping steadily into the channel — sustains them
Dew collects in the channel overnight

questions.question: The river does not rise the moment the rain starts because:
options: Water needs time to travel from the hills to the gauge — the lag time
Rain first evaporates completely
The gauge only reads once a day
Rivers rise before the rain arrives

questions.question: The three questions for interpreting any hydrograph are:
options: How wide, how deep, how muddy
How high the peak, how soon after the rain, how steep the climb
How long, how cold, how fast
Which river, which town, which month

questions.question: After a storm, base flow settles slightly higher than before because:
options: The channel has widened permanently
The gauge drifts upward
Stormwater drains keep discharging for weeks
The recharged soil now feeds the channel more generously

subtopics.title: Laingsburg and eThekwini — Lessons From Real Floods

questions.question: At Laingsburg in 1981, the catchment answered like a corrugated roof because:
options: It was covered in wetlands
The town had paved its entire catchment
Bare rock and baked Karoo soil could absorb almost nothing of the extreme rain
The Buffels River was dammed upstream

questions.question: In the April 2022 eThekwini floods, the deaths were concentrated in:
options: Informal settlements on steep slopes and low riverside land
High-rise city-centre buildings
Coastal hotels
Farming districts inland

questions.question: The pair of floods illustrates the two flood characters as:
options: Both were slow regional floods
Laingsburg the spike-hydrograph flash flood; eThekwini the broad, sustained regional flood
Both were flash floods lasting minutes
eThekwini the flash flood; Laingsburg the regional flood

questions.question: The remedies read off the hydrograph all aim to:
options: Shorten the lag and raise the peak
Stop rain from falling on catchments
Replace rivers with canals
Lengthen lag time and lower the peak — sponges restored, floodplains respected, drains maintained, warnings issued
